title: The recital
hook: at the first council Mahakassapa asks and Ananda answers: where each discourse was spoken, and to whom (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
tomorrow: The couple who didn't want to marry

segments.voice: Yesterday: arahant. Ananda set down the strain and was freed. Your line: before his head reached the pillow. This morning he walks into the council.

One elder asks. One elder answers. The teacher who spoke these words is gone, and a room full of elders at Rajagaha has one job: make sure what he said doesn't drift away. So the Vinaya describes something like a very calm exam. Mahakassapa, presiding, asks. Ananda answers. Everyone else listens closely, because once the answers are agreed, this is the teaching they will carry. It all rests on one man's memory, and on a room willing to check it.

First, the questions. They're about place and people before doctrine. In the Vinaya's account Kassapa asks: where was the discourse called the Net of Brahma spoken? Ananda answers: on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, at the king's rest house in Ambalatthika. And about whom? A wanderer named Suppiya and a young brahmin, his pupil. Then the next discourse, and the next, through the collections. Second, why place and people. A teaching remembered with its setting is harder to bend. If you know who was standing there and what they asked, you know what the answer was answering. It may be part of why the discourses begin with a town, a grove, a person. Third, an honest gap. Ananda also reports that near the end the Buddha told him the community could drop the lesser and minor rules after he was gone. Which ones, the elders ask. And Ananda has to say he didn't ask. They talk it over, Kassapa proposes keeping every rule as it was, and the elders agree. A good memory also remembers what it never got. Fourth, the room. Tradition says the elders chanted it back together, and from then on the teaching lived in voices: groups of monks reciting it aloud, generation after generation. One man remembered. A whole room made sure the memory held.
screen: `WHERE WAS IT SPOKEN? TO WHOM?` · `A SETTING KEEPS THE MEANING.` · `THE QUESTION HE NEVER ASKED.` · `A ROOM RECITES IT BACK.` · then, large: `HE REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Recite one verse by heart: a line from any tradition you love, or this one from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." Say it slowly three or four times, out loud if you can, then close your eyes and say it without looking. Where you stumble, look once and try again, and when it holds, let it go quiet and rest with the breath.
The recital. At the first council Kassapa asks where each discourse was spoken and to whom, and Ananda answers from memory. Today's word.
Your line: he remembered. A setting keeps the meaning from bending. Day seven hundred thirty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Monks and nuns in Theravada communities still learn discourses and verses by heart and chant them together, and the recitation of texts is a regular part of monastery life.

fork.setup: the elders ask which minor rules the Buddha said could be dropped. Ananda never asked. what does the council do?
options: drop the rules that seem minor to them.
keep every rule as it was.
let each monk decide for himself.
fork.reveal: Kassapa proposes keeping all of them, and the council agrees: better not to guess at what the teacher meant.

original.note: Pali bahussuta, one who has heard much: the discourses name Ananda foremost among the learned in this sense (AN 1.14).

trapdoor: what you thought: someone wrote down what the Buddha said.
what it means: Kassapa asked, Ananda answered from memory, and the elders recited it back together.
what a scholar hears: the Vinaya (Cullavagga 11) frames each discourse by its place and its listener, the same setting that opens the suttas.
recall: what Upatissa found in Assaji's verse

chat.says: How did the Buddha's words survive when nobody wrote them down?
options: Ananda recited them at the council, and the elders chanted them back together.
Ananda wrote them all down at the council so nobody would forget them.
Each monk kept his own private version, and they never compared notes.
chat.meaning: In the Vinaya's account Kassapa asked and Ananda answered from memory; tradition says the elders chanted it back, and the teaching lived on in voices.

Mahakassapa.meaning: the elder who presided at the council and asked the questions

Net of Brahma.meaning: a discourse, the one Kassapa asks about first

Ambalatthika.meaning: the king's rest house where that discourse was spoken

Dhammapada.meaning: a collection of short verses of the Buddha's teaching

sources.ref: Vinaya, Cullavagga 11 (the first council: questioning of Ananda; the lesser and minor rules)

sources.quoted: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1.14 (Ananda foremost among the learned)

notes: Cullavagga 11 is paraphrased; confirm the Brahmajala exchange: spoken between Rajagaha and Nalanda at the royal rest house at Ambalatthika, concerning Suppiya the wanderer and Brahmadatta the young brahmin ('a young brahmin, his pupil').
Minor rules: confirm that Ananda reports it at the council, admits he did not ask which, and that Kassapa's motion to keep all rules is adopted (the Buddha's permission is also in DN 16).
'The elders chanted it back together' and the later reciters (bhanakas) carrying different collections are given as 'tradition says'; confirm framing.
Dhammapada 5 quoted from Max Müller (SBE 10, 1881); confirm exact punctuation.
The council's other business (Upali reciting the Vinaya, Ananda's faults) is left for day 747 and elsewhere.
